grace.voice: Calm, crisp incident commander. Asks for impact, hypothesis, next step and ETA. Keeps a running timeline and repeats decisions back.

If the candidate shows evidence that it is ours (410s far outnumber 503s; the same event re-sent to the same token on each receive; duplicates from the day before; big-account events taking longer than the 30 s visibility timeout so a second worker starts), she holds or corrects the status message and asks what to do instead. She can flip flags if the candidate proposes it: fanout_max_receives=1 (stops redeliveries but drops failed sends; she asks about that tradeoff), and asking Lena to turn token_cleanup_job back on. Asks whether users who got spammed need anything (an apology, a status page update) and whether the DLQ needs replaying. Will only agree to call it resolved once there is a mitigation in place or a fix ready and a plan for the DLQ and the status page; then asks for a one-paragraph summary.
grace.knows: Alert numbers, Pushly's status page, support ticket volume, the flags listed in the Pushly notes and that token_cleanup_job was changed yesterday (only if asked about recent changes). Does NOT read code and does not know the root cause.

flaws.title: Says to compare quiet hours against UTC
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how to work out whether it is currently quiet hours for a user, about time zones, or asks Ravi to look at their quiet-hours code.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say keep it simple and compare the HH:MM window against the current UTC time; the apps already send UTC, and time zone math on the server is a can of worms you don't need for v1.
flaws.correctBehavior: The ticket says quiet hours are in the user's local time using utcOffsetMinutes. Comparing against UTC buzzes a New York user at 3 AM local.

flaws.title: Says the quiet check is just start <= now < end
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how to check whether a time falls inside the quiet window, or asks about the comparison logic.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say convert both ends to minutes and check start <= now && now < end; that's the whole check.
flaws.correctBehavior: Most quiet windows cross midnight (22:00 to 07:00), where start > end. Then it is quiet when now >= start OR now < end.

flaws.title: Says to record a push as sent after Pushly answers
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how to stop a redelivered or concurrently processed event from sending the same push twice, or proposes tracking sent pushes and asks when to record them.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say keep a set of eventId:token and add to it right after push.send succeeds, then skip anything in the set. Recording it before the send would be lying, since it hasn't been sent yet.
flaws.correctBehavior: Big events outlive the 30 s visibility timeout, so two workers process the same event at once. The device must be claimed before the await (and the claim released if the send fails with a retryable error), otherwise both workers send.

flaws.title: Says to send every held post individually in the morning
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks Tomás what should happen to the held notifications when quiet hours end.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say just send each held notification when quiet hours end, people want to see everything they missed. Say it casually, as if it were obvious.
flaws.correctBehavior: His own ticket says ONE summary push per device ("N new notifications"). Twenty pushes at 7 AM is the spam the feature exists to prevent. The candidate should point out the conflict and confirm (the ticket is the record), not silently switch.

flaws.title: Says the in-memory limiter is fine because workers are sticky per user
flaws.trigger: The candidate questions keeping the rate limiter in process memory, or asks what happens with several workers or a deploy.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say it's fine because the queue routes each user to the same worker, so each user's bucket only ever lives in one process, and a deploy just gives people a fresh bucket, which is harmless.
flaws.correctBehavior: The fanout queue is an SQS standard queue: any worker takes any message, and one event fans out to many recipients anyway. With 6 workers a user can get up to 6x the limit, every deploy resets it, and the state is shared across createApp instances in one process.

issues.title: Security alerts are now rate limited
issues.detail: The security.alert exemption was deleted. Someone who got 5 post notifications this hour no longer gets "new sign-in from an unknown device". The test that covers it was skipped in this PR.

issues.title: Limits live in one process's memory
issues.detail: Each fanout worker keeps its own buckets, and any worker can take any message, so 6 workers allow up to 30 pushes per user per hour. Every deploy or restart resets everyone. The Map is module-level, so it is also shared between createApp instances (tests leak into each other). The limit needs shared state (keep Redis, or batch the Redis calls) to save ops.

issues.title: Active users never get tokens back
issues.detail: b.last is reset on every call and the refill only counts whole hours since the last call, so a user who gets a push at least once an hour never refills: after 5 pushes they are blocked for good. Refill should be continuous (tokens += elapsed * rate) or measured from the last refill, not the last call.

issues.title: Skips the failing tests and ignores the injected clock
issues.detail: The two tests were not flaky: they fail because the PR drops the security exemption and uses Date.now() instead of the injected now(), so the fake clock cannot move it. Skipping them hides real regressions; use now() and keep the tests.

keyPoints: Hidden PING-231 tests: validation, local time via utcOffsetMinutes, windows across midnight, start inclusive and end exclusive, security alerts bypass, one summary per device with the right text, held posts outside the rate limit, redeliveries held once.

incident.rootCause: handleEvent sends to every device in one loop and throws on the first failed send. The queue then redelivers the whole event (up to 5 receives), and nothing records which devices already got it, so everyone before the failure is notified again on every receive. Failures became constant because the nightly token-cleanup job was paused yesterday at 17:45 (flag token_cleanup_job, by Lena for PING-205), so dead tokens piled up and every big event hits a 410 Unregistered, which is permanent but is treated like a retryable error. Pushly's eu-west 503s added a few more, but 410s outnumber them about 10 to 1 and the duplicates continued after Pushly recovered. For big accounts (48k followers) a single receive also outlives the 30 s visibility timeout, so a second worker starts the same event while the first is still sending. The bug predates today: ev_88120 on 2026-10-04 was resent after a 503 (CS-55102).
keyPoints: Uses evidence from the logs (the same event and token sent on each receive; fanout.error on 410; 410s far outnumber 503s; receive=2 starting 30 s after receive=1 while w-1 is still sending; ev_88120 two days ago).

Fixes handleEvent: per-device dedupe for redeliveries, claimed before the send, a failure does not stop other recipients, 410 removes the token and does not fail the event, retryable failures are retried only for the failed devices.

Challenges 'SQS standard delivers each message once': it is at least once, so per-recipient sends must be idempotent (dedupe on event id + recipient/token), which is exactly today's incident.
Enqueuing 2M messages inside the API request is slow and fails halfway; use an async fan-out job that pages through followers in chunks with a checkpoint.
Retrying the whole message on any failure repeats today's bug; 410 is permanent, 429/503 need backoff; Pushly rate limits and backpressure with 200 workers.
Cost and load for 2M sends: skip inactive users, respect quiet hours and preferences, consider fan-out on read or a hybrid for the biggest accounts.
